title: Third stage of labour and cord clamping
blurb: Explain active and physiological third stage, choose a safe uterotonic, time cord clamping and recognise a prolonged third stage under NICE NG235.
question: Amara, 31, para 2, has just given birth on a midwife-led unit and chose active management of the third stage. She had pre-eclampsia in this pregnancy. Which uterotonic should the midwife give, and when should the cord be clamped?

teach.h: The third stage: birth of the baby to birth of the placenta
teach.body: Formally (NICE NG235 1.10.2): the third stage of labour is the time from the birth of the baby to the expulsion of the placenta and membranes. In plain English: the baby is out, and now the uterus must separate and deliver the placenta, then clamp down to stop bleeding. The midwife's job is to keep this safe while protecting the first meeting between the woman, her companions and the baby, minimising separation and disruption (1.10.1).

rows.label: Cord
values: Clamped and cut after 1 min, before 5 min
Not clamped until pulsation stops or placenta out

teach.caption: Active management is associated with a lower risk of postpartum haemorrhage and blood transfusion (1.10.6).

teach.h: Her choice, informed by her risk
teach.body: Discuss both options antenatally, at initial assessment and in labour, including benefits and risks (1.10.5). Advise that active management lowers the risk of PPH and transfusion (1.10.6). If a woman requests physiological management, discuss her level of risk so she can make an informed decision, and support her choice (1.10.7). Document the agreed decision (1.10.8). Observations in the third stage: her colour, respiration, her own report of how she feels, and vaginal blood loss (1.10.3).

head: Option
Route
Key point
rows: If oxytocin was used in labour
May be more effective; more nausea and vomiting
teach.caption: Give immediately after the birth of the baby and before the cord is clamped and cut.

teach.h: Is oxytocin plus ergometrine safe for her?

children.edge: Severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, or severe cardiac, hepatic or renal disease
children.label: Oxytocin alone

children.edge: None, and PPH risk factors present
children.label: Oxytocin + ergometrine advised

teach.caption: NG235 1.10.9-1.10.10: oxytocin plus ergometrine is advised when risk factors raise PPH risk; offer an antiemetic such as cyclizine.

items.label: Clamp and cut the cord
items.sub: not earlier unless cord integrity concern or HR < 60 not rising

items.label: Clamp to allow controlled cord traction
items.sub: support her if she asks for later clamping

teach.caption: Record the timing of cord clamping in both active and physiological management (1.10.16).

teach.h: When to change from physiological to active
items: Advise a change if there is haemorrhage (1.10.17).
Advise a change if the placenta is not delivered within 1 hour of the birth (1.10.17).
Offer a change if the woman wants to shorten the third stage (1.10.18).
Retained placenta: secure IV access and explain why; no umbilical vein agents; IV oxytocics only if she is bleeding excessively; no manual removal without anaesthetic (1.10.21-1.10.28).

teach.h: Worked scenario: Amara on the midwife-led unit
teach.body: Amara chose active management. Because she has pre-eclampsia, oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated, so the midwife gives oxytocin 10 units IM straight after the birth, before clamping. The cord is clamped and cut after at least 1 minute and before 5 minutes, then controlled cord traction is used once there are signs of separation. If the placenta is not delivered within 30 minutes, this is a prolonged third stage and the retained placenta pathway begins.

teach.text: Do not mix up the two clocks: prolonged third stage is over 30 minutes with ACTIVE management but over 60 minutes with PHYSIOLOGICAL management. And controlled cord traction belongs to active management, only after the uterotonic and signs of separation.

items: Third stage = birth of baby to expulsion of placenta and membranes.
Active: uterotonic, clamping after 1 and before 5 minutes, CCT after separation; lowers PPH risk.
Oxytocin 10 units IM is standard; oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in severe hypertension and pre-eclampsia.
Do not clamp before 1 minute unless the cord is damaged or HR is under 60 and not rising.
Prolonged: over 30 min (active) or over 60 min (physiological).

summary: You can now explain active and physiological management of the third stage, choose a uterotonic that is safe for the woman in front of you, and time cord clamping correctly. You can also recognise a prolonged third stage and the first steps for a retained placenta.

A.q: A midwife is explaining the third stage of labour to a student. Which definition is correct?
options: From full dilatation of the cervix until the baby is fully born
From the birth of the placenta to the end of the first hour
From the start of active pushing to the birth of the placenta
From birth of the baby to expulsion of placenta and membranes
A.why: NG235 1.10.2 defines the third stage as the time from the birth of the baby to the expulsion of the placenta and membranes.

whyNot.0: Full dilatation to the birth of the baby is the second stage of labour.
whyNot.1: The third stage ends with the expulsion of the placenta and membranes, not an hour later.
whyNot.2: Active pushing belongs to the second stage; the third stage starts once the baby is born.

A.q: Grace, 27, chose active management of the third stage. She has no medical problems and no oxytocin was used in labour. Which uterotonic is most appropriate?
options: Oxytocin 5 units by slow IV injection after the placenta
Ergometrine 500 micrograms IV once the cord has been cut
Oxytocin 10 units IM after birth, before cord clamping
Carbetocin by slow IV injection after the birth
A.why: NG235 1.10.11: for active management after vaginal birth give oxytocin 10 units IM (or one of the listed alternatives) immediately after the birth of the baby and before the cord is clamped and cut.

whyNot.0: Slow IV oxytocin 5 units is for women who received oxytocin in labour, and the uterotonic is given before clamping, not after the placenta.
whyNot.1: Ergometrine is given with oxytocin as an IM injection; IV ergometrine alone is not an NG235 active management option.
whyNot.3: Carbetocin is recommended for women who have had a caesarean birth (1.10.13).

A.q: During active management, when should the midwife clamp and cut the cord of a healthy term baby?
options: After at least 1 minute and before 5 minutes
Immediately, so the uterotonic can act
After pulsation stops and the placenta delivers
Within 30 seconds, to start cord traction early
A.why: NG235 1.10.14: do not clamp earlier than 1 minute from the birth unless there is a cord integrity concern or HR under 60 that is not rising; clamp before 5 minutes to perform controlled cord traction.

whyNot.1: Immediate clamping is not recommended for a healthy baby; wait at least 1 minute.
whyNot.2: Waiting for pulsation to stop or for the placenta describes physiological management.
whyNot.3: Clamping within 30 seconds is earlier than NICE allows for a healthy baby.

B.q: Sunita, 35, has severe hypertension in labour and requests active management of the third stage. Which uterotonic should the midwife avoid?
options: Oxytocin 10 units IM
Oxytocin 5 units by slow IV injection
Oxytocin plus ergometrine IM
Carbetocin after a caesarean birth
B.why: NG235 1.10.9: oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, or severe cardiac, hepatic or renal disease.

whyNot.0: Oxytocin 10 units IM is suitable and is not contraindicated by hypertension.
whyNot.1: Slow IV oxytocin is an option, particularly if oxytocin was used in labour; it is not contraindicated here.
whyNot.3: Carbetocin is offered after caesarean birth; hypertension is not the listed contraindication.

B.q: Jo, 29, chose a physiological third stage. Forty minutes after the birth her placenta has not delivered, she is not bleeding heavily and is well. What is the most accurate description?
options: A prolonged third stage needing the retained placenta pathway
A prolonged third stage needing manual removal now
Within the expected time for a physiological third stage
An indication for umbilical vein oxytocin injection
B.why: NG235 1.10.20: a physiological third stage is prolonged if not completed within 60 minutes. At 40 minutes with no haemorrhage she is within the expected time; a change to active management is advised if the placenta is not delivered within 1 hour (1.10.17).

whyNot.0: The 30-minute limit applies to active management; for physiological management the limit is 60 minutes.
whyNot.1: It is not yet prolonged, and manual removal must never take place without anaesthetic (1.10.28).
whyNot.3: Umbilical vein agents are not used for a retained placenta (1.10.22).

B.q: During a physiological third stage, Leah, 33, starts bleeding heavily. What should the midwife advise?
options: Continue physiological management and massage the uterus
Change to active management of the third stage
Wait until 60 minutes before giving any uterotonic
Clamp the cord and begin cord traction straight away
B.why: NG235 1.10.17: advise a change from physiological to active management if there is haemorrhage or the placenta is not delivered within 1 hour.

whyNot.0: Haemorrhage is one of the two triggers to change to active management, not to continue.
whyNot.2: Haemorrhage is a trigger in its own right; there is no need to wait for 60 minutes.
whyNot.3: Controlled cord traction is performed only after a uterotonic has been given and there are signs of separation (1.10.15).

C.q: Priya, 30, received an oxytocin infusion in labour and has now given birth vaginally. She chose active management and has no contraindications to any uterotonic. If oxytocin alone is chosen, how should it be given?
options: 10 units by rapid IV bolus
5 units by slow IV injection over 3 to 5 minutes
5 units by IM injection after the placenta
10 units added to the infusion running at that time
C.why: NG235 1.10.11-1.10.12: oxytocin is given IM, or by slow IV injection of 5 units over 3 to 5 minutes for women who have received oxytocin during labour.

whyNot.0: A rapid IV bolus of 10 units is not recommended; the IV dose is 5 units given slowly.
whyNot.2: The uterotonic is given immediately after the birth of the baby, before cord clamping, not after the placenta.
whyNot.3: Adding oxytocin to the labour infusion is not the NG235 third-stage regimen.

C.q: Immediately after birth, Baby Okafor has a heart rate of 50 beats per minute that is not increasing. Ade, the mother, had planned to have the cord clamped late. What should the midwife do about the cord?
options: Wait at least 1 minute before clamping as planned
Clamp and cut the cord without waiting a full minute
Wait until pulsation has stopped, as Ade requested
Milk the cord towards the baby, then clamp at 5 minutes
C.why: NG235 1.10.14 permits clamping earlier than 1 minute when the baby has a heart rate below 60 that is not getting faster, so that resuscitation can begin.

whyNot.0: The 1-minute minimum does not apply when the heart rate is under 60 and not rising.
whyNot.2: Waiting for pulsation to stop would delay resuscitation of a baby whose heart rate is under 60.
whyNot.3: Cord milking is not part of NG235 third-stage care, and delaying until 5 minutes would delay resuscitation.

C.q: Hannah, 38, para 4, had active management with oxytocin 10 units IM. Thirty-five minutes later the placenta has not delivered, she is bleeding normally and her observations are stable. She is in a freestanding midwifery unit. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give IV oxytocin to deliver the placenta
Inject oxytocin into the umbilical vein
Arrange transfer and secure IV access
Attempt manual removal with Entonox
C.why: This is a prolonged third stage (over 30 minutes with active management, 1.10.20). For a retained placenta, secure IV access and explain why (1.10.21); if she is not in an obstetric unit, arrange transfer (1.10.27).

whyNot.0: IV oxytocics are not used routinely for a retained placenta; they are given if the woman is bleeding excessively (1.10.23-1.10.24).
whyNot.1: Umbilical vein agents should not be used for a retained placenta (1.10.22).
whyNot.3: Uterine exploration or manual removal must not be carried out without an anaesthetic (1.10.28).

reteach.title: Two clocks, one decision
reteach.question: If you remember just one thing about the third stage, it is that the package she chooses sets the clock. How do the two packages differ step by step?

blocks.body: Active management is a package: a uterotonic straight after the birth, clamping between 1 and 5 minutes, then controlled cord traction once the placenta has separated. Physiological management is the opposite package: no routine drug, no clamping until pulsation stops or the placenta is out, and she pushes the placenta out herself. Active gives a lower risk of PPH, so she needs that information to choose.

steps.label: Baby born
steps.sub: Skin-to-skin, observe her colour and loss

blocks.text: Ergometrine raises blood pressure: that is why oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. Use oxytocin alone for these women.

explain.body: Active management: routine uterotonic, cord clamped and cut, controlled cord traction after signs of separation. Physiological: no routine uterotonic, no clamping until pulsation stops or after the placenta, placenta delivered by maternal effort. Active management lowers the risk of PPH and transfusion.

test.q: Which component belongs to physiological management of the third stage?
options: Controlled cord traction after separation
Routine IM oxytocin after the baby's birth
Clamping the cord at 2 minutes after birth
Placenta delivered by maternal effort
test.why: In physiological management the placenta is delivered spontaneously or by maternal effort (NG235 1.10.2).

whyNot.0: Controlled cord traction is part of active management.
whyNot.1: A routine uterotonic is the defining feature of active management.
whyNot.2: Clamping between 1 and 5 minutes belongs to active management; physiological management waits for pulsation to stop or the placenta.

explain.body: Oxytocin 10 units IM is the standard choice. Oxytocin plus ergometrine may be more effective at reducing PPH, is advised when PPH risk factors are present, but causes more nausea and vomiting (offer an antiemetic) and is contraindicated in severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, or severe cardiac, hepatic or renal disease.

test.q: Mei, 34, has PPH risk factors and no medical conditions. She chooses active management. What should the midwife offer alongside oxytocin plus ergometrine?
options: A second uterotonic dose at 15 minutes
Paracetamol for uterine cramps
Tranexamic acid as prophylaxis
An antiemetic such as cyclizine
test.why: Oxytocin plus ergometrine is more likely to cause nausea and vomiting, so NG235 1.10.10 recommends offering antiemetics, for example cyclizine.

whyNot.0: There is no routine second prophylactic dose in NG235.
whyNot.1: Paracetamol is not the NG235 recommendation linked to this drug; the specific side effect is nausea and vomiting.
whyNot.2: Tranexamic acid in NG235 is a treatment for PPH (1.10.35), not routine prophylaxis.

explain.body: Do not clamp earlier than 1 minute from the birth unless there is concern about the integrity of the cord or the baby has a heart rate below 60 that is not getting faster. In active management clamp before 5 minutes to allow controlled cord traction, but support a woman who asks for later clamping. Record the timing.

test.q: Which finding allows the cord to be clamped earlier than 1 minute?
options: The woman has had a previous PPH
The baby is crying with good tone
The cord appears to be torn
The woman chose active management
test.why: NG235 1.10.14 allows earlier clamping if there is concern about the integrity of the cord, or a heart rate below 60 that is not getting faster.

whyNot.0: Previous PPH affects the choice of uterotonic, not the minimum time to clamping.
whyNot.1: A crying baby with good tone is healthy: wait at least 1 minute.
whyNot.3: Active management still includes waiting at least 1 minute before clamping.

explain.h: Prolonged third stage and retained placenta
explain.body: Prolonged if not completed within 30 minutes (active) or 60 minutes (physiological). Secure IV access and explain why. Do not use umbilical vein agents. IV oxytocics only if bleeding excessively. Transfer if not in an obstetric unit. No manual removal without anaesthetic.

test.q: After active management, Rosa's placenta has not delivered at 35 minutes and she is bleeding excessively. Which drug action is appropriate?
options: Umbilical vein oxytocin injection
Intravenous oxytocic agents
A second dose of oxytocin into the cord
Oral misoprostol to expel the placenta
test.why: NG235 1.10.24: give intravenous oxytocic agents if the placenta is retained and the woman is bleeding excessively.

whyNot.0: Umbilical vein agents are not used for a retained placenta (1.10.22).
whyNot.2: Injection into the cord is an umbilical vein agent, which NICE advises against.
whyNot.3: Oral misoprostol to expel a retained placenta is not an NG235 recommendation.
